The evidence suggests that screening or surveillance for primary hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with ultrasonography can improve the prognosis of patients. Ultrasonographic screening has been shown to reduce mortality from HCC and may provide early detection of the disease.

In terms of specific findings, a study demonstrated that patients who underwent ultrasonographic screening had better disease-free survival rates compared to those who did not receive screening. Another study found that selective embolization (a procedure used to treat HCC) contributed to improved survival in patients with HCC.

However, it's essential to note that the overall yield of ultrasonography for detecting HCC was low (7%), and accuracy was lower when percutaneous liver biopsy was not implemented. Additionally, the use of ultrasonography as a standalone procedure for staging HCC may be less effective than other diagnostic methods, such as laparoscopy.

Therefore, while the evidence suggests that screening or surveillance with ultrasonography can improve prognosis, it's crucial to consider individual patient factors and diagnostic accuracy when deciding on an approach.
